facts: Jensen Huang resigned as Nvidia CEO on Nov. 12 following reports of extramarital affairs, including one with a woman alleged to have ties to Chinese intelligence.
Nvidia's board reinstated Huang as CEO on Monday, 11 days after his resignation, saying it believed he was the right person to lead the company.
Nvidia's stock closed at $165.05 per share Monday, up roughly 31.5% from Friday's close of $125.53, with BBC reporting about $1 trillion added to the company's market value.

ladder.analysis: Nvidia, the world's second-most-valuable company, sits at the center of the global AI buildout and the U.S.-China technology rivalry, with its chips powering major AI systems used by Google, Meta, Amazon, Microsoft and others. Huang's abrupt resignation and rapid reinstatement — reversing the board's prior public insistence that he would not return — unfolded alongside a roughly 31.5% stock rebound, underscoring how closely Nvidia's market value, and by extension financing across the AI sector, is tied to Huang personally. The episode intertwines corporate governance, national security concerns over chip exports to China, and direct presidential involvement, setting up congressional scrutiny of both Nvidia and the administration's role in the reversal.

Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) said Nvidia should have moved on without Huang and criticized the administration's push to save him, arguing the U.S. cannot pursue the AI race while giving China its best technology.

ladder.steelman: Across party lines, lawmakers are converging on the same underlying worry — not necessarily Huang's personal conduct, but whether U.S. chip export policy and oversight of Nvidia are robust enough given the company's outsized role in AI infrastructure and national security.

facts: President Trump delivered remarks at the Department of Justice on Monday, appearing alongside Attorney General Todd Blanche and FBI Director Kash Patel, with the White House billing the speech as focused on 'protecting American families' and specifically on Gov. Gavin Newsom's (D-Calif.) death penalty commutations.
On Nov. 5, Newsom announced his intention to commute all 548 California death sentences to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole.

Because the affected inmates have multiple felony convictions, California law requires a recommendation from the state Supreme Court before the commutations can take effect; Newsom's administration has said it will not proceed until the court acts, and has asked the justices to rule before his term ends in January.

A coalition of California prosecutors and victims' advocates petitioned the state Supreme Court to halt the plan, arguing Newsom did not give victims' families an opportunity to be heard; the court has invited additional briefs through Nov. 24.

California voters rejected ballot measures to abolish the death penalty in both 2012 and 2016; the state has not carried out an execution since 2006, and Newsom imposed a formal moratorium on capital punishment shortly after taking office in 2019.

The White House provided a list of 20 condemned inmates who would benefit from the commutations, including Marcus Wesson (murder of nine family members), Richard Allen Davis (murder of Polly Klaas, 12), and Isauro Aguirre (torture-murder of Gabriel Fernandez, 8).

On his first day back in office, Trump directed the DOJ to prioritize seeking and implementing lawful death sentences, and in April the department announced measures including reinstating its lethal injection protocol and expanding execution methods.
Trump's DOJ appearance was notable as a rarity for a sitting president; his previous visit to the department was in March 2025.
ladder.analysis: This story centers on a clash between executive clemency power and a legal/political fight over capital punishment in California. Under the state constitution, governors retain clemency authority even when voters have preserved the death penalty by referendum, and Newsom is invoking that authority for inmates he argues received sentences that cannot be squared with justice, while the California Supreme Court must sign off given the inmates' multiple felony records. The dispute has become a national flashpoint because it pits a Democratic governor's use of individual clemency against a Republican president's broader law-and-order agenda, with Trump using a DOJ platform—paired with federal officials and highly publicized, graphic case details—to cast Newsom's move as a betrayal of crime victims rather than a legal or moral debate about capital punishment itself.

stories.headline: COP31 climate talks collapse without deal, first failure in 17 years
body: The longest UN climate summit in history collapsed without a final deal on Sunday in Antalya, Turkey, marking the first such failure in 17 years. The proposed Antalya Pact fell apart after countries failed to agree on language regarding fossil fuels and climate finance, exposing deep divisions in a geopolitical environment described by Australian minister Chris Bowen, who led the negotiations, as 'the most complicated and fraught geopolitical environment in living memory.'

The central dispute centered on whether the pact would explicitly commit to moving away from fossil fuels, the main driver of global warming. Three years ago at COP28 in Dubai, nations agreed to transition away from fossil fuels, but the Antalya Pact omitted any mention of them. Countries that rejected the pact argued that without that explicit commitment, the new agreement would weaken the Dubai accord. About 130 governments—roughly two-thirds of those represented—backed a demand for explicit language on moving away from fossil fuels, but oil-producing nations led opposition. Saudi negotiator Mohammad Ayoub, speaking for 22 Arab League countries, said Arab nations had contributed less than 2% of historical greenhouse gas emissions and defended their right to choose their own climate actions. Russia's delegate Sergei Kononuchenko warned that cutting oil and gas supplies before demand falls would cause shortages and energy poverty, stating, 'For that reason, we cannot agree to any formulation on fossil fuel.'

The collapse also reflected a broader geopolitical backdrop. The United States, which had previously helped broker compromises, had no official delegation in Antalya after President Donald Trump rejected the international climate process. While delegates argued over fossil fuels, Trump, China's President Xi Jinping, and Russia's Vladimir Putin issued a joint declaration in Shenzhen pledging to increase production and supply of refined petroleum products. Turkey's environment minister and summit president Murat Kurum criticized governments for getting 'hung up on one word or phrase' while people desperate for climate action were disappointed.

Climate finance was another major sticking point. Kononuchenko complained that much of the money wealthy countries provide to poorer nations comes as loans rather than grants, calling it 'an old colonial distribution of labour under a new banner.' Many developing countries share this grievance, arguing they are asked to pay for damage they did little to cause while receiving insufficient help to adapt. The EU had ruled out significant new funding before the talks began. Kenyan campaigner Mohamed Adow of Power Shift Africa accused Europe of rejecting a flawed deal while refusing to acknowledge its own responsibility for the finance failure. Uganda's environment minister Beatrice Atim Anywar, whose country faces deadly landslides, floods, and droughts, told DW that climate financing for developing countries to deal with impacts has not materialized, saying, 'This is a thing we are living with.'

Despite the failure, the final draft of the Antalya Pact had contained remarkably strong language expressing 'deep concern' that global warming was expected to exceed 1.5°C in the next few years and warning of increasingly serious, irreversible damage. That language survived without provoking opposition, but countries could not agree on how to respond. Christiana Figueres, who led the UN negotiations that delivered the Paris Agreement, argued that countries were right to walk away rather than endorse a weaker commitment that might undermine progress. UN climate chief Simon Stiell acknowledged the need to 'improve, modernise and reform' the process. Some governments have proposed introducing voting when consensus proves impossible, but the UN climate process depends on consensus because international cooperation is largely voluntary. The failure does not halt climate action—solar panels, batteries, and electric vehicles are becoming more competitive—but the energy transition is not moving fast enough for the climate.

stories.headline: Ukraine war spills into NATO territory as attacks reach Libya and Baltic
body: The war between Russia and Ukraine has again spilled into NATO territory, with a Russian cargo ship struck by a drone in the Baltic Sea over the weekend and Russian cruise missiles landing in Poland last week, while Ukrainian drones also hit Russian naval assets off the coast of Libya, according to reports from NPR and CNN.

On Saturday, a drone struck the Russian cargo ship Sparta II in the Gulf of Finland, setting it ablaze. Russia took control of the vessel and towed it out of Finnish waters a day later, after the crew was rescued by another Russian ship. The attack is presumed to have come from Ukraine, but Kyiv has not claimed responsibility. Finnish President Alexander Stubb called the incident an "unfortunate reminder" that the consequences of Russia's war are visible in the region. Teams from Finland and Estonia helped Russian ships extinguish the fire, and Stubb thanked them for their "responsible and professional actions." The Sparta II transports weapons and other supplies to Russia for use against Ukraine; the vessel is under U.S. and U.K. sanctions, and its owner is under European Union sanctions. Finland chose not to seize the ship, citing the risk of a major environmental hazard if it sank. Jukka-Pekka Lumilahti, director of sea operations for the Finnish Border Guard, said, "If we would let the vessel burn, it would most likely sink. And after that, it would cause a major environmental risk for Finland and Estonia."

Last Friday, Russia launched three cruise missiles that landed between 30 and 60 miles from a military exercise in Poland involving nearly a dozen countries, which was training forces for a potential peace-monitoring mission in post-war Ukraine. Multiple air alerts were issued, and participants were told to take cover. NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte, asked in Warsaw whether the alliance could stop such incursions, said, "I cannot guarantee you that it will not happen. But I can guarantee you is that NATO will defend every inch of Polish territory, that as a collective alliance, we impose immense costs on Russians." NATO ambassadors were scheduled to meet Monday in a special session to discuss further measures to protect Poland.

Ukraine also struck Russian naval assets near the port of Benghazi, Libya, according to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, hitting a Russian naval ship and a cargo vessel. The strikes showcase Kyiv's ability to reach Russian assets in the Mediterranean. Meanwhile, Russia launched what Zelensky called the most intense attack of the year on Friday — a six-hour barrage of drones and missiles that struck bridges and power infrastructure across Ukraine, killing dozens and leaving swaths of the country and capital in blackout.

The widening theater of conflict comes amid a stalled peace process. President Donald Trump has called Russian President Vladimir Putin his friend, and the U.S. has reframed talks as being about wider European security infrastructure — a long-standing Russian goal. Putin stated in Shenzhen that Russia has no interest in negotiating a ceasefire, and he added that if Europeans want to join talks, they should travel to Moscow to make their case. The Kremlin has also accused Lithuania of allowing a drone to fly through its airspace — NATO territory — to strike the Sparta II, an allegation that feeds Russia's fiction that it is at war with all of NATO. The two sides' demands are moving further apart, with the Kremlin reportedly wanting NATO to fall back westward and the U.S. reportedly floating Ukraine's NATO membership — incompatible red lines. As CNN noted, "You can't expect nonsense talks to ever stop the real business of killing."

stories.headline: Israeli strikes kill UNRWA worker in Gaza; Oxfam report calls enclave a toxic wasteland
stories.byline: International & World desk · anchored on Reuters
body: Israeli air strikes killed at least three people in Gaza on Monday, including Adel al-Helo, a worker for the UN Palestinian refugee agency UNRWA, according to the agency and local health officials. UNRWA said al-Helo was working near a water well in the Jabalia refugee camp in the north of the enclave when he was hit; three others were wounded in the strike. Later on Monday, another Israeli air strike targeted a vehicle in western Gaza City, killing two people and wounding others, medics said. The Israeli military did not immediately comment. The strikes came despite an October 2025 ceasefire deal with Hamas that formally halted around two years of fighting but has not ended Israel's genocidal war on Gaza, Al Jazeera reported. Since the ceasefire, at least 1,679 Palestinian people and five Israeli soldiers have been killed. Israeli forces have also continued to destroy residential buildings beyond the 'Yellow Line' to which they were required to withdraw under the ceasefire; Mohammed Musleh, mayor of Deir el-Balah's Maghazi municipality, told Al Jazeera that more than 500 housing units had been destroyed in less than a month, describing what he called a systematic policy of gradual creeping displacement.

Separately, the charity Oxfam released a report describing Gaza as 'a toxic wasteland,' saying more than 99% of the Palestinian territory shows indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks. Heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and dioxins and biological contaminants pose threats now and potentially for decades, the report said. Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data. The report notes that all six wastewater treatment plants in Gaza are out of operation, with untreated sewage flowing into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea; heavy winter storms have recently caused rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people. It cites a February statement by a UN special rapporteur that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years, 'the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs.' Last year, the UN Environment Programme estimated that Israel's military operations had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris, with about 15% potentially carrying a high risk of hazardous contamination.

Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC that 'there are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment.' She said Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage, and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths. Gazan doctors have already reported increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and from displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard, while gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation. Palestinian dermatologist Dr Alaa Abu Hajar told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the war began, attributing it to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic conditions in tents and displacement camps: 'There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets. Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children.' Fishermen say untreated sewage and rubble dumped into the sea have harmed marine life; fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan said, 'Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster... When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage.' Testing of contamination levels is often impossible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and Israeli restrictions block specialist testing equipment and scientists, the BBC reported.

Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, said the impact on Gaza 'will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival.' He accused Israel of 'environmental war crimes' as part of an 'ongoing genocide in Gaza.' Israel has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted, maintaining that its military campaign is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, and that it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm. The Israeli embassy in the UK sharply criticised the Oxfam report, saying it 'falls short of professional standards' and relies on satellite imagery 'and unverified assumptions, and its methodology lacks the academic rigour needed to withstand serious scrutiny.' It argued the report drew conclusions about Gaza's soil and groundwater without considering the excavation of hundreds of kilometres of tunnels by Hamas, rendering it fundamentally flawed. The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up, with special attention to protecting workers involved.

At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. The UN says humanitarian conditions remain dire. UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed, speaking Monday ahead of the International Day of Solidarity with the Palestinian People, said the war has undone 77 years of human development in Gaza, according to a joint UN-World Bank assessment. She condemned 'the abhorrent terror attacks by Hamas on 7 October 2023' but added that 'nothing can justify the collective punishment of the Palestinian people.' She called for unhindered humanitarian access and protection for aid workers, saying 'aid must never be obstructed, diverted, or used as a bargaining chip,' and urged political and financial support for UNRWA. She stressed that recovery must be Palestinian-led, with women and youth playing a meaningful role, and that reconstruction cannot substitute for a political solution: 'The Occupied Palestinian Territory must remain politically, economically, and territorially integrated – and united under a single, legitimate, sovereign, democratic Palestinian Government.' She reaffirmed UN support for two states, Israel and Palestine, living side by side along pre-1967 lines as 'the only vital path forward.' Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups; in July, Hamas accepted a US-led Board of Peace plan to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal, but the Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

Israeli forces have continued to destroy residential buildings beyond the 'Yellow Line' to which they were required to withdraw under the ceasefire.
Mohammed Musleh, mayor of Deir el-Balah's Maghazi municipality, told Al Jazeera that more than 500 housing units had been destroyed in less than a month.
Musleh described what he called a systematic policy of gradual creeping displacement.
The charity Oxfam released a report describing Gaza as 'a toxic wasteland.'
The Oxfam report says more than 99% of the Palestinian territory shows indicators of environmental contamination from Israeli military attacks.
Heavy metals, explosive residues, asbestos from destroyed buildings, and dioxins and biological contaminants pose threats now and potentially for decades, according to the Oxfam report.
Oxfam and the UK-based Conflict and Environment Observatory (CEOBS) used satellite imagery, remote sensing, spatial analysis and other open-source data for the report.
All six wastewater treatment plants in Gaza are out of operation, according to the Oxfam report.
Untreated sewage is flowing into groundwater and the Mediterranean Sea, according to the Oxfam report.
Heavy winter storms have recently caused rainwater to mix with wastewater and flow through streets and tent sites housing displaced people, according to the Oxfam report.
The Oxfam report cites a February statement by a UN special rapporteur that more than 200,000 tonnes of explosives were dropped on Gaza in almost two years.
The UN special rapporteur's statement equated the explosives to 'the equivalent of the total energy of approximately 13 Hiroshima-type nuclear bombs.'
Last year, the UN Environment Programme estimated that Israel's military operations had generated more than 61 million tonnes of debris.
The UN Environment Programme estimated that about 15% of the debris potentially carries a high risk of hazardous contamination.
Oxfam report author Lama Abdul Samad told the BBC that 'there are going to be chronic health impacts that are long term because a lot of these contaminants are persistent in the environment.'
Samad said Gazans are likely to suffer from increased respiratory diseases, cancers, organ damage, and a rise in birth defects and stillbirths.
Gazan doctors have already reported increased acute respiratory infections caused by dust and pollution from destroyed buildings and from displaced people burning plastic, rags and cardboard.
Gastrointestinal diseases are linked to unsafe water and poor sanitation, according to the report.
Palestinian dermatologist Dr Alaa Abu Hajar told the BBC he had seen a five-fold increase in chronic skin diseases since the war began.
Dr Hajar attributed the increase to environmental pollution and overcrowded, unhygienic conditions in tents and displacement camps.
Dr Hajar said: 'There are rodents, rubbish and sewage that's spread through the streets. Unfortunately, the age group most affected is children.'
Fishermen say untreated sewage and rubble dumped into the sea have harmed marine life.
Fisherman Abu al-Abed Sultan said: 'Sewage and wastewater are discharged into the sea without treatment and this is a great disaster... When we lower our nets, we catch rubble and garbage.'
Testing of contamination levels is often impossible because Gazan laboratories have been destroyed and Israeli restrictions block specialist testing equipment and scientists, the BBC reported.
Oxfam International's executive director, Amitabh Behar, said the impact on Gaza 'will have fundamentally degraded the environmental conditions necessary for human safety and survival.'
Behar accused Israel of 'environmental war crimes' as part of an 'ongoing genocide in Gaza.'
Israel has rejected genocide accusations in an ongoing case at the International Court of Justice as baseless and distorted.
Israel maintains that its military campaign is an act of self-defence against Hamas in response to the group's deadly attack on Israel on 7 October 2023.
Israel says it takes steps to mitigate civilian harm.
The Israeli embassy in the UK sharply criticised the Oxfam report, saying it 'falls short of professional standards.'
The embassy said the report relies on satellite imagery 'and unverified assumptions, and its methodology lacks the academic rigour needed to withstand serious scrutiny.'
The embassy argued the report drew conclusions about Gaza's soil and groundwater without considering the excavation of hundreds of kilometres of tunnels by Hamas, rendering it fundamentally flawed.
The Oxfam report calls for a full, independent environmental assessment to identify contamination risks ahead of a clean-up, with special attention to protecting workers involved.
At least 74,746 Palestinians have been killed since the start of the war in Gaza, according to the Hamas-run health ministry.
The UN considers the health ministry's figures reliable.
The UN says humanitarian conditions remain dire.

UN Deputy Secretary-General Amina Mohammed, speaking Monday ahead of the International Day of Solidarity with the Palestinian People, said the war has undone 77 years of human development in Gaza, according to a joint UN-World Bank assessment.
Mohammed condemned 'the abhorrent terror attacks by Hamas on 7 October 2023.'
Mohammed added that 'nothing can justify the collective punishment of the Palestinian people.'
Mohammed called for unhindered humanitarian access and protection for aid workers, saying 'aid must never be obstructed, diverted, or used as a bargaining chip.'
Mohammed urged political and financial support for UNRWA.
Mohammed stressed that recovery must be Palestinian-led, with women and youth playing a meaningful role.
Mohammed said reconstruction cannot substitute for a political solution.

Mohammed said: 'The Occupied Palestinian Territory must remain politically, economically, and territorially integrated – and united under a single, legitimate, sovereign, democratic Palestinian Government.'
Mohammed reaffirmed UN support for two states, Israel and Palestine, living side by side along pre-1967 lines as 'the only vital path forward.'
Israel has conditioned large-scale Gaza reconstruction on the full disarmament of Hamas and other armed groups.
In July, Hamas accepted a US-led Board of Peace plan to give up its weapons in exchange for an Israeli troop withdrawal.
The Israeli government said the proposal was insufficient.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang's return as Nvidia CEO sparks massive stock market rally
body: U.S. stocks surged on Monday in their best day since April 2025 after Nvidia reinstated Jensen Huang as CEO, reversing a steep sell-off that had pushed the major averages into correction territory. The S&P 500 jumped 4.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average rose more than 1,400 points (about 3%), and the Nasdaq Composite rallied nearly 6.5%. The rally was led by Nvidia, whose stock soared 31% — its biggest one-day gain since May 2003 — adding more than a trillion dollars in market capitalization, a record for any public company, according to Bespoke Investments.

The move came after Nvidia's board announced it had reinstated Huang as president, CEO and board director, effective immediately. Board chair Harvey Jones said, "The Board believes Jensen is the right person to lead NVIDIA, and that his reinstatement is in the best interests of our stockholders, employees, partners and customers." President Trump said he spoke with the board and "convinced" members to bring Huang back after he was forced to resign following reports of affairs, including one that intelligence officials had previously leaked to the media as potentially involving a Chinese spy.

The relief rally followed a brutal week that saw the S&P 500 and Dow enter correction territory. The S&P 500 alone tumbled more than 9% between Huang's initial departure on Nov. 12 and Friday's close. Wall Street experts were divided on whether the bounce marks a lasting bottom. Mark Gibbens, founder of Gibbens Capital Management, said, "I think the AI trade is back on. I certainly believe this establishes a bottom and a floor in the AI trade and the recent market weakness." Art Hogan, chief market strategist at B. Riley Wealth Management, noted that futures were already higher Sunday night before any news of Huang's return, suggesting the market was oversold. "Sometimes you just hit that crescendo where you know the market gets oversold, and I would argue that we'd be higher today, even without the Nvidia news," he said.

But other strategists urged caution. Jay Woods, chief market strategist at Freedom Capital Markets, said the rally may fizzle because "people will pull back and still have the same questions we had before he was replaced." Nomura cross-asset strategist Charlie McElligott warned that much of the move was driven by "mechanical" buying — short sellers being forced to cover their bets and options dealers unwinding hedges — and said it would be "naïve to believe that a one-day 'Up Shock' absolves the market of underlying concerns." Peter Boockvar, chief investment officer at One Point BFG Wealth Partners, said the "picks and shovels" AI trade will remain dependent on the rate of capital expenditure spending by hyperscalers. "That, at the end of the day, is the story that those companies are going to have to deal with outside of bounces like we're seeing now," he said.

The sell-off that began before Huang's departure was driven by broader concerns: worries about financing the AI buildout, data center approvals after Democratic wins in the midterm elections, and fears that hyperscaler capital expenditure may have peaked. Those issues remain unresolved. Traders at Goldman Sachs summed up the market's dependence on Nvidia's fate with a note: "Not sure yet whether good or bad that the fate of the market is almost equal to the fate of one person. But hey ... We are not picky here."

Elsewhere in markets, Oatly stock surged as much as 108% after Belgian investment company Verlinvest increased its stake to roughly 42.6%, purchasing the interest from China Resources. Jefferies initiated coverage of SpaceX with a Buy rating and a $210 price target, citing AI rather than rockets as the main value driver. The broader tech rally also lifted SpaceX shares more than 7% in sympathy with the sector.

stories.headline: Mets sign Tarik Skubal to record $450M contract, then add Paul Goldschmidt
body: The New York Mets signed left-handed pitcher Tarik Skubal to a nine-year, $450 million contract and followed it within 24 hours by agreeing to a one-year, $8 million contract with first baseman Paul Goldschmidt, according to multiple reports. The Goldschmidt deal, reported by Robert Murray of FanSided and confirmed by Will Sammon of The Athletic, includes up to $2 million in incentives, per Joel Sherman of the New York Post. Because the Mets are a perennial luxury-tax payor in the highest penalty tier, the $8 million base salary will be taxed at 110 percent, bringing the total cost to approximately $16.8 million.

Goldschmidt, 39, spent the 2026 season with the New York Yankees, appearing in 105 games and totaling 380 plate appearances. He hit .252/.343/.452 with 18 home runs, 13 doubles, a triple, a 7.6 percent walk rate and a 22.6 percent strikeout rate. All of his production came against left-handed pitching: in 183 plate appearances versus southpaws, he slashed .299/.393/.573, while against right-handers he managed just .213/.239/.351 in 197 plate appearances. Defensively, he posted two defensive runs saved and five outs above average in 623 1/3 innings at first base, according to FanGraphs.

The Mets’ need at first base arose after Pete Alonso departed in free agency following the 2025 season, signing a five-year, $155 million contract with the Baltimore Orioles. New York pivoted to sign Jorge Polanco to a two-year, $40 million deal, but Polanco played only 37 games in 2026 and slashed .148/.201/.230/.431. The Mets have a platoon option in Jared Young, who hit .266/.330/.429 in 342 plate appearances last season but struggled against left-handers. Young also has corner outfield experience and could move to a bench role.

Sherman, writing for the New York Post, said the Goldschmidt signing follows a pattern of the Mets acquiring former Yankees. "They needed a right-hander who hits left-hand pitching well to play first base, and Goldschmidt still does that, even in the upper-30s," Sherman said. "He still plays first base defensively at a high level, though not the same level he did in his prime Gold-Glove age. He's New York proven. The Mets are trying to improve their clubhouse culture continuously. Goldschmidt works to that. Just a solid dude."

The Mets have added more than $50 million in salary for 2027 between Skubal and Goldschmidt, plus a $45 million signing bonus for Skubal, with total luxury-tax obligations exceeding $111 million. In the previous 48 hours, the club also signed center fielder A.J. Ewing to an eight-year, $95 million extension. President of baseball operations David Stearns is expected to continue reshaping the roster, with potential trade candidates including Kodai Senga, Jorge Polanco and Mark Vientos. The Mets finished last in their division in 2026 after a late-season collapse in 2025.

stories.headline: Pochettino's Man Utd slide continues after Liverpool thrashing
body: Mauricio Pochettino's reign as Manchester United head coach began in desperate fashion on Sunday as his 10-man side were thrashed 4-0 by Liverpool at Anfield, leaving United second from bottom of the Premier League and in the relegation zone. Liverpool fans sang that Pochettino would be "sacked in the morning" after 15 minutes, by which point his team were already 2-0 down and had been reduced to 10 men. United midfielder Kobbie Mainoo summed up the mood afterward, telling MUTV: "We're at the lowest we've ever been and no-one's coming to save us. There are no helping hands coming, so we've got to work together, lean on each other, keep working and hopefully it will come good. It's all about character now."

The defeat extended a dire run in which United have conceded 19 goals in their past six games and have kept only one clean sheet all season, against Azerbaijani champions Sabah FK in September. Pochettino's big selection decision at Anfield was to pick Matthijs de Ligt in the centre of a three-man defence ahead of Harry Maguire. De Ligt made his first appearance in 11 months in a 4-1 loss at Como on 21 October following major back problems that required surgery, and he played only two minutes against Roma on 3 November. His failure to deal with a high ball at Anfield presented Alexander Isak with a clear run at goal and prompted Leny Yoro to make the tackle that led to his controversial dismissal, which Pochettino felt shaped the 82 minutes that followed.

Pochettino shut down a question about United's poor recent defensive record after the match, saying: "Tell me only about the circumstance today. I wasn't [here] in the past." He acknowledged his reasoning for picking De Ligt, saying, "He played in the Champions League you know, before the internationals," though it was not clear which match he meant. United have nine games before the January transfer window opens, including home matches against Coventry, Nottingham Forest and Sunderland, a trip to Crystal Palace on 13 December, and Champions League fixtures against Sporting on Wednesday and RB Leipzig on 8 December. Newly promoted Coventry are four points above United, while Forest and Sunderland occupy the two positions immediately above the Old Trafford club; Crystal Palace are the only side below United.

United's options are limited by injuries and squad issues. Their only recognised number nine, Benjamin Sesko, is out at least until January with a shin problem that has bothered him since March, making a striker Pochettino's reported priority. First-choice left-back Luke Shaw missed his eighth successive game on Sunday, and the only other orthodox left-back in the senior ranks, England Under-20 international Harry Amass, did not make the bench at Anfield. Pochettino worked with Shaw at Southampton early in his career and feels the 31-year-old can be a positive influence on his group. Summer arrival Carlos Baleba is injured for the second time since the start of pre-season, and there are doubts over £48m Brazilian midfielder Andrey Santos, who went five games between Premier League starts under Carrick from the opening-day defeat at Hull and was only introduced for the final three minutes at Anfield.

The club borrowed from their revolving credit facility around their major summer purchases and again earlier this month when Pochettino was hired at a cost of just over £7.5m. Public accounts released last week confirmed United have another £160m available in credit but owe £417m in outstanding transfer fees, £236m of which is due within 12 months. Chief executive Omar Berrada has said the club needs to be "disciplined" in the transfer market and avoid spending huge sums on players who would not necessarily make the squad better. There was sympathy with former boss Michael Carrick's belief that he had been let down in the summer transfer window, and a plan to address that situation remains in place.

United supporters travelling to Lisbon for Wednesday's Champions League match expressed resigned acceptance punctuated by dark humour about a possible relegation to the Championship and whether Manchester City might join them there. Former United winger Ashley Young, a Premier League winner with the club, told Match of the Day: "They have got enough in that squad to get themselves out of the bottom three. They have not been showing that, but Pochettino has only just come in. He is going to want to get his team set up in a way that they are hard to beat. Right now, they do not look like they are hard to beat. It doesn't look like there is that togetherness. He has got to find a way to get that out of them." The new regime has decided on warm-down sessions at Carrington after matches, a change from Carrick's tendency to give starting players a day off, with defensive organisation a key focus ahead of the Sporting match. United's last relegation came in 1973-74 under Tommy Docherty, and confidence remains high at Old Trafford that the situation will not become that dire, but as the BBC noted, it could be a very bumpy ride.

stories.headline: UK to host 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa confirms
body: England, Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales will jointly host the 2035 Women's World Cup, Fifa has confirmed, marking the first time a football World Cup has been held in the United Kingdom since the men's tournament in 1966. The four countries were the only bidders for the tournament and were ratified as co-hosts at a specially arranged virtual meeting from Fifa's Zurich headquarters. The tournament will consist of 104 matches contested by 48 teams over 39 days.

The 'All Together' bid proposed using 19 venues: 14 in England, one in Northern Ireland, two in Scotland and two in Wales. English stadiums listed in the bid are Villa Park, The Amex, Ashton Gate, Elland Road, Hill Dickinson Stadium, Emirates Stadium, Selhurst Park, Tottenham Hotspur Stadium, Wembley, Etihad Stadium, St James' Park, the City Ground, the Stadium of Light and Old Trafford. If Manchester United's proposed new Old Trafford stadium does not go ahead, the current stadium would still be considered. The Welsh venues are Cardiff City Stadium and Principality Stadium, with Easter Road in Edinburgh and Hampden Park in Glasgow in Scotland. A redeveloped Windsor Park is set to stage matches in Northern Ireland. Three more stadiums could be added — Birmingham's new Powerhouse Stadium, Wrexham's redeveloped Racecourse Ground and a potential new Chelsea ground — which would take the tournament to 16 cities and 22 venues.

Fifa's special meeting also approved the joint bid by Mexico, the United States, Costa Rica and Jamaica to host the 2031 finals, which will be the first to feature 48 teams. Fifa has yet to decide whether all four UK co-hosts will qualify automatically. The news came on the same day the UK government announced a vision for one million more girls to play, watch or be in leadership roles in sport by the time the tournament takes place.

England failed to win the right to host the men's World Cups in 2006 and 2018, and a proposed UK and Ireland bid for the 2030 tournament was abandoned. England and Scotland hosted matches at the men's Euros in 2021, and England staged the women's European Championship in 2022, which the Lionesses won. England, Scotland, Wales and the Republic of Ireland will jointly host the men's European Championship in 2028.

Football Association chief executive Mark Bullingham said: "Hosting Euro 2022 allowed us to change the game in our country, by creating a generation of aspirational role models and growing demand from women and girls to play. Hosting a World Cup would give us the chance to build on that across all four nations." Football Association of Wales chief executive Noel Mooney called it "a proud day for Welsh football", while Irish Football Association chief executive Patrick Nelson said the event "would be felt in every club and every age group, in every part of the country". Scottish Football Association chief executive Ian Maxwell said hosting would be "the most significant thing to happen to the women's and girls' game in Scotland".

The participation of women and girls in football has risen by 2.3 million since the Women's European Championship was held in England in 2022, but women remain underrepresented in leadership positions: only a quarter of chief executive, chair or performance director roles in major UK sports are held by women, and only 12% of sports federations are led by a woman. Fifa's evaluation, published earlier this month, rated the bid 4.3 out of five. Its contractual framework was rated 'medium risk', and the document said "certain government guarantees contain material qualifications, particularly regarding tax and safety and security" — a reference to a lack of agreement over Fifa's request for tax-free status for all football-related activities. The evaluation added that "certain contractual matters remain subject to further discussion", but that "the bidder's proactive engagement with Fifa and the substantial lead-in time provide a sound basis for resolving these outstanding issues".

stories.headline: FDA approves first drug for limb-girdle muscular dystrophy, BridgeBio’s Welgemda
body: The Food and Drug Administration on Monday approved the first drug to treat limb-girdle muscular dystrophy (LGMD), a group of progressive genetic muscle conditions that had previously had no approved therapy. The drug, developed by BridgeBio and marketed as Welgemda (also known as BBP-418), is specifically approved for adult and pediatric patients with LGMD type 2I/R9 who weigh at least 30 kg (66 lbs). BridgeBio estimates the subtype affects 2,000 to 3,000 patients in the U.S. and another 4,000 to 5,000 in Europe, with about 7,000 people in the U.S. and Europe living with LGMD2I/R9 or other addressable alpha-dystroglycanopathies. The company said it will charge insurers $75,446.58 for a 28-day supply, putting the price just under $1 million per year.

Acting FDA Commissioner Kyle Diamantas called the approval "a historic milestone" for patients and families, adding that under the Trump Administration’s commitment to accelerating innovation and removing barriers for rare disease therapies, the FDA is "proud to deliver real hope and meaningful progress for patients who have waited far too long for options." Laura Jawidzik, director of the Division of Neurology 2 in the FDA’s Center for Drug Evaluation and Research, said in a prepared statement: "Limb-girdle muscular dystrophy is a progressive muscle disease that gradually takes away a patient’s ability to walk, breathe, and live independently, often beginning in childhood. The clinical data supporting Welgemda's approval show meaningful improvements in walking speed and lung function, and we are encouraged by what that can mean for patients' daily lives."

LGMD2I/R9 is an autosomal recessive disease caused by mutations in the FKRP gene that reduce levels of the encoded protein, impairing a cellular process called glycosylation and ultimately destabilizing and damaging muscles. Welgemda is an oral glycosylation substrate therapy designed to deliver supraphysiological levels of substrate to the partially functional FKRP enzyme, enhancing residual enzyme activity to restore glycosylation of alpha-dystroglycan (αDG), a common biomarker for the disease. There are more than 30 subtypes of LGMD, and Welgemda is the first targeted treatment for any form of the disease. Individuals homozygous for the L276I variant typically develop symptoms in late childhood; in adulthood, about 25% lose independent ambulation, 10% need assisted ventilation, and 30% develop cardiomyopathy. Other FKRP genotypes typically present earlier and more severely, with cardiac involvement in about 60% of patients and pulmonary failure by age 30 in nearly all cases.

The approval was supported by a prespecified 12-month interim analysis of the Phase 3 FORTIFY trial, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled 36-month study that enrolled 112 symptomatic, genetically confirmed LGMD2I/R9 patients aged 12 to 60 years (18 to 60 in Europe), including both ambulatory and nonambulatory patients. At the interim analysis, 74 participants had been assigned to Welgemda and 38 to placebo; about 74% of each arm were homozygous for the L276I variant. The trial met its primary interim endpoint, showing a statistically significant 1.8-fold increase in glycosylated αDG from baseline at month 3 (P < .001), sustained through month 12 (P < .001 vs placebo), with levels rising from 22.7% to 44.5% of control in the treatment group versus about 20% with placebo. Welgemda also met secondary endpoints, including an 82% reduction in serum creatine kinase (a biomarker for muscle damage), with a least squares mean difference versus placebo of −2055.6 U/L (P < .001). On the 100-meter timed test, walking velocity improved by 0.14 m/s with Welgemda and declined by 0.12 m/s with placebo, a between-group difference of 0.27 m/s (P < .001). Forced vital capacity (FVC), a measure of lung function, increased by about 3% predicted with treatment, a difference of about 5% predicted versus placebo (P = .007). Effects were consistent across subgroups defined by genotype, age, and baseline FVC.

The safety profile showed diarrhea as the most common treatment-emergent adverse event, reported in 39.2% of the Welgemda group and 52.6% of the placebo group; all cases were grade 1 or 2. Grade 3 or 4 treatment-emergent adverse events occurred in 5.4% and 5.3% of the groups, respectively. There were no discontinuations due to adverse events, no deaths, and no treatment-related serious adverse events. The company noted that gastrointestinal effects such as diarrhea and stomach pain, along with joint pain, are among the most common adverse reactions. The approval was largely expected, with Jefferies analyst Andrew Tsai giving the therapy higher than 90% odds of approval by the FDA’s November 27 deadline, based on FORTIFY results. BridgeBio has identified more than 500 prospective patients in the U.S. while guiding toward potentially thousands more with adequate genetic testing and diagnosis, and Tsai predicted a market opportunity of greater than $1 billion annually at peak sales.

The approval rests on interim data from an ongoing trial, and whether early biomarker and functional gains translate into delayed loss of ambulation, ventilatory dependence, or cardiac events will require longer follow-up. The cardiac findings were exploratory and based on small subgroups, and absolute functional changes, while statistically significant, were measured over 12 months in a slowly progressive disease. Data are also lacking in children younger than 12; BridgeBio plans to begin a study in that population in the first half of 2027, along with studies in LGMD2M/R13 and LGMD2U/R20. The drug previously received FDA orphan drug, fast track, and rare pediatric disease designations. BridgeBio submitted its new drug application in March 2026, and the FDA granted priority review without convening an advisory committee. The approval is the first of three expected rare disease drugs from BridgeBio, which is also developing infigratinib for achondroplasia (with an FDA target action date of February 4, 2027) and the ATTR-CM drug Attruby.

stories.headline: FDA approves giredestrant, first new early-stage breast cancer hormone therapy in over 20 years
body: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration on Nov. 23 approved giredestrant (Wilserdly) as an adjuvant treatment for adults with early-stage hormone receptor (HR)-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, marking the first new endocrine therapy for this setting in more than 20 years. The approval, announced by manufacturer Genentech, covers stage I, II, or III disease with an intermediate to high risk of recurrence following surgery. It comes one week after the FDA approved giredestrant in combination with everolimus for adults with ER-positive, HER2-negative, ESR1-mutated locally advanced or metastatic breast cancer, making giredestrant the first selective estrogen receptor degrader (SERD) indicated for both early- and advanced-stage disease.

The early-stage approval was supported by the international phase 3 lidERA trial, which enrolled 4,170 people with HR-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either giredestrant or one of several standard endocrine therapies for up to five years. After a median follow-up of about 32 months, patients receiving giredestrant had a 30% lower risk of invasive disease recurrence or progression than those receiving standard endocrine therapy (hazard ratio, 0.70; 95% CI, 0.57-0.87; P = .0014), with 140 versus 196 events in the respective groups. The risk of distant disease, meaning cancer that had spread to another part of the body, was reduced by 31%. At three years, 92.4% of giredestrant-treated patients were alive and free of invasive breast cancer versus 89.6% of those receiving standard therapy, translating to about 28 additional patients per 1,000 remaining free of invasive breast cancer. Overall survival data were immature but showed a positive trend; the trial will continue to follow participants, with Genentech committing to submit the data to the FDA as a postmarketing requirement.

Giredestrant belongs to a newer class of drugs called selective estrogen receptor degraders, or SERDs. Rather than simply blocking estrogen's interaction with the receptor, the drug is designed to bind to the estrogen receptor and promote its breakdown, cutting off a major driver of tumor growth. About 70% of breast cancers are hormone receptor-positive, meaning cancer cells have receptors that allow hormones such as estrogen to promote their growth. For people with early-stage HR-positive, HER2-negative breast cancer, surgery is often followed by endocrine therapy—typically tamoxifen or an aromatase inhibitor, often taken for five years or longer—to reduce the chance of recurrence. Recurrence remains a concern, and some patients struggle with side effects during years of treatment.

The safety profile of giredestrant was broadly similar to standard endocrine therapy. Common side effects included muscle and joint pain, hot flashes, fatigue, headache, and nausea, most of which were low grade; common laboratory abnormalities included increased liver enzyme levels, decreased blood cell counts, and elevated blood lipid levels. Fewer patients receiving giredestrant discontinued treatment due to adverse events compared with those receiving standard hormone therapy (5.3% versus 8.2%). Women who have not completed menopause are instructed to receive an additional hormone-suppressing medicine alongside giredestrant; men may also receive this medicine depending on a health care provider's input.

The lidERA trial was led by Aditya Bardia, MD, director of the Breast Oncology Program and professor of medicine at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA, and director of translational research integration at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center, who presented the results at the San Antonio Breast Cancer Symposium in December 2025. "This is a very significant development and perhaps one of the most important breast cancer advances in recent years for hormone receptor-positive disease," Bardia said. "As clinicians, our goal is always to prevent recurrence and help patients live longer, healthier lives and this brings us closer to that." Levi Garraway, MD, PhD, chief medical officer and head of global product development at Genentech, said in a news release that by "addressing a critical need in early-stage disease, where the chance for cure is greatest, [giredestrant] has the potential to establish an important new standard of care for patients and physicians." Teresa Graham, chief executive officer of Roche Pharmaceuticals, said the company will "continue to invest in the broad development of [giredestrant], exploring its potential across different stages of the disease and in new treatment combinations."

The approval was also welcomed by clinicians and patients. Rena Callahan, MD, clinical professor of medicine at the David Geffen School of Medicine at UCLA and an investigator in the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center, recommended that her patient Jeanette Barbosa consider participating in the lidERA trial. Barbosa, now 52, was initially diagnosed with stage 2 invasive lobular breast cancer; surgery revealed the disease was more extensive, including cancer in her lymph nodes, and her diagnosis was upgraded to stage 3. After chemotherapy and radiation, she sought a second opinion at UCLA Health, where she met Callahan. "From the very beginning, when I walked in her office, I just felt so hopeful," Barbosa said. "We just felt like we landed in the right spot. I didn't feel defeated. I felt like she was handing me my life back." Callahan noted that with standard treatment, about a third of patients with high-risk breast cancer experience a recurrence. Barbosa said she participated not only for herself but for other women: "I didn't just do this for myself. I'm doing it for other women, too, to potentially combat cancer for the rest of our lives." She reported minor side effects and occasional low energy that have been manageable and have not prevented her from living her normal life, including fostering puppies and kittens and spending time with family.

stories.headline: Oldest known quasar pair discovered from cosmic dawn
body: Astronomers have discovered the oldest known compact pair of quasars, dating back to just 900 million years after the Big Bang. The system, designated J1602+4228AB and given the Hawaiian name Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, is powered by two supermassive black holes with masses of approximately 1.5 billion and 400 million times the mass of the Sun. The pair also holds the record for the closest separation between two known quasars from the cosmic dawn era, at roughly 18,100 light-years apart — about one-fifth the diameter of the Milky Way. The discovery is described in a paper published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, led by Silvia Onorato, a postdoctoral research associate at NSF NOIRLab.

The quasars were first identified in data from the Aether survey, a James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) research program that used the Near-Infrared Spectrograph Integral Field Unit to observe 200 quasars — about 43% of all known quasars from this early period. While visually examining the survey data, researchers noticed that a previously known quasar, J1602+4228A, appeared to have a companion. Follow-up observations using the Gemini North telescope on Maunakea in Hawai‘i, equipped with the Gemini Near-Infrared Spectrograph (GNIRS), allowed the team to distinguish the two objects individually. The team also used Gemini North’s Gemini Multi-Object Spectrograph (GMOS) to gather additional data and rule out the possibility that the second object was a mirage caused by gravitational lensing; spectral differences between the two objects favor the interpretation that they are separate physical quasars, though further lensing modeling is needed.

Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is only the third known quasar pair from cosmic dawn, and its black holes are so massive at such an early epoch that existing theories cannot definitively explain their growth. “There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our Universe, much less two,” Onorato said. “We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the Universe was only a thirteenth of its age and astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today.” The researchers believe the pair may have formed in an unusually dense region of the early Universe, where frequent galaxy interactions supplied enormous amounts of gas, accelerating both star formation and black hole growth.

The Hawaiian name Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua was developed through the A Hua He Inoa program, a collaboration involving the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center of Hawaiʻi and the University of Hawai‘i’s Ka Haka ʻUla O Keʻelikōlani (Hawaiian Language College). The name was created by professor Larry Kimura and translates to “Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the Universe.” Its components describe the system’s physical characteristics: Nā (plural), Pō (fathomless powerful darkness, symbolizing the black holes), Wawā (reincarnation or procreation), ʻEna (brilliance of heat, describing the intense radiation from accreting matter), and Kaulua (double or pair). The name also connects to earlier astronomical objects named through the program, including Pōwehi (associated with the first image of a black hole in 2019) and Pōniuāʻena (the most distant known quasar when discovered in 2020).

The discovery was made possible by combining observations from JWST and Gemini North, which is operated by NSF NOIRLab as part of the International Gemini Observatory. The team benefited from exceptionally favorable observing conditions on Maunakea, with clear skies and unusually sharp atmospheric conditions allowing them to gather the necessary data in just two nights. “The sky over Maunakea was so clean and sharp that we managed to collect the data in only two nights,” Onorato said. The quasar pair offers a unique laboratory for studying how the earliest massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled through direct galaxy interactions during cosmic dawn.

Silvia Onorato said: 'We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the Universe was only a thirteenth of its age.'
Silvia Onorato said: 'Its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today.'
The researchers believe the pair may have formed in an unusually dense region of the early Universe.
In that dense region, frequent galaxy interactions supplied enormous amounts of gas.
The gas accelerated both star formation and black hole growth.
The Hawaiian name Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua was developed through the A Hua He Inoa program.
The A Hua He Inoa program is a collaboration involving the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center of Hawaiʻi and the University of Hawai‘i’s Ka Haka ʻUla O Keʻelikōlani (Hawaiian Language College).
The name was created by professor Larry Kimura.
The name translates to 'Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the Universe.'

The name's components describe the system’s physical characteristics: Nā (plural), Pō (fathomless powerful darkness, symbolizing the black holes), Wawā (reincarnation or procreation), ʻEna (brilliance of heat, describing the intense radiation from accreting matter), and Kaulua (double or pair).
The name connects to earlier astronomical objects named through the program, including Pōwehi (associated with the first image of a black hole in 2019).
The name also connects to Pōniuāʻena (the most distant known quasar when discovered in 2020).
The discovery was made possible by combining observations from JWST and Gemini North.
Gemini North is operated by NSF NOIRLab as part of the International Gemini Observatory.
The team benefited from exceptionally favorable observing conditions on Maunakea.
The conditions included clear skies and unusually sharp atmospheric conditions.
The team gathered the necessary data in just two nights.
Silvia Onorato said: 'The sky over Maunakea was so clean and sharp that we managed to collect the data in only two nights.'
The quasar pair offers a unique laboratory for studying how the earliest massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled through direct galaxy interactions during cosmic dawn.

stories.headline: Jensen Huang reinstated as Nvidia CEO after scandal, pressure from Trump and tech allies
body: Jensen Huang returned to Nvidia as CEO and president on Monday, less than two weeks after resigning amid reports of affairs including with an alleged Chinese spy. The board reinstated him after receiving input from senior levels of the U.S. government and determining that his return poses no national security risk. Nvidia stock rose about 30 percent in early trading following the announcement, recovering some of the roughly 25 percent decline since Huang's resignation.

Huang resigned on November 12 after admitting he was "unfaithful to my wife" and that he "created problems for the board." Reports had detailed affairs with Alice Huang, an executive at Nvidia customer Megaspeed who was allegedly enlisted by Chinese intelligence to spy on Nvidia, and with Nvidia vice president of healthcare Kimberly Powell. The board initially said it would not reinstate him, but a pressure campaign mounted by tech leaders and President Donald Trump changed the outcome.

Trump said he was "totally involved" in Huang's reinstatement. Vice President JD Vance worked over the weekend with Huang and the board to resolve the situation, and Trump called into a board meeting to advocate for Huang's return. The board formed a National Security and Export Control Committee and is seeking a chief compliance officer. The Securities and Exchange Commission is investigating Nvidia's accounting practices, and the Justice Department is investigating Megaspeed for potentially smuggling AI chips to China.

Tech leaders celebrated Huang's return. Elon Musk called it "the mistake has been corrected," having previously likened Huang's departure to "kicking Michael Jordan off your team when you're on a winning streak." OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, who was himself fired and reinstated nearly three years ago, posted "Jensen!" Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney called Huang's return "a demonstration of American resiliency." Binance co-founder Changpeng Zhao and former Uber CEO Travis Kalanick also voiced support.

Huang returned to Nvidia's office to a crowd of applauding employees. "Thank you all for the second chances. I'm gonna be a better CEO the second time around," he said. "This is my first day at work. I'm terribly sorry for putting all of you through all of this." The board said it will finish its investigation into Huang, and Sen. Elizabeth Warren called the reinstatement "reckless," urging the administration to explain the input government officials provided.

stories.headline: Amazon to acquire Decart's AI optimization tech for $7.5B ahead of Trainium sales push
body: Amazon has agreed to acquire a significant portion of Israeli startup Decart for $7.5 billion, according to Bloomberg, as the tech giant prepares to sell its Trainium AI chips to customers. The deal, announced in an Amazon blog post, includes the technology behind Decart's Decart Optimization Stack (DOS), software that helps AI models run efficiently on hardware from Nvidia, Amazon, and Google, as well as Decart's founding team and its roster of AI researchers and engineers.

Decart is known for building interactive real-time world models—most recently Oasis 3—and AI video-generation tools. DOS is designed to maximize the efficiency of AI workloads across different hardware platforms.

“Every leap forward in AI starts with getting more out of every chip,” said Peter DeSantis, Amazon's SVP of foundational AI models, custom silicon, and quantum computing. “More efficient compute means better training, better reinforcement learning, faster inference, and better models for customers at a lower cost.”

Amazon has so far used its Trainium chips internally at its own data centers, but is now preparing to sell them to customers as a direct competitor to Nvidia's offerings, which have been the industry standard. Decart's technology could make it easier for customers to run their workloads on Amazon chips instead of Nvidia's, lowering the barrier to adoption.
Neither Decart nor Amazon immediately responded to requests for comment.

stories.headline: CrowdStrike to acquire Zscaler for $43.9 billion in all-stock deal
body: Cybersecurity giant CrowdStrike has agreed to acquire Zscaler in a $43.9 billion all-stock deal, the companies announced Monday. The transaction is expected to create what the companies described as the 'largest single addressable market' for cybersecurity, positioning them for the AI era.

Zscaler, based in San Jose, California, provides cloud cybersecurity products to approximately 8,000 enterprise companies. Its core offering is zero-trust technology, a security feature that requires employees to authenticate each time they access an internal system or resource, designed to prevent hackers from stealing credentials and gaining unfettered network access.

CrowdStrike secures the computers, laptops, phones, and other devices connected to a company's network. The companies said the deal will unite CrowdStrike's endpoint protection software with Zscaler's zero-trust platform to better defend customers against data breaches, offering 'superior protection' by combining the two products.
In remarks on Monday, the companies said the acquisition will help customers safely adopt AI. The deal is subject to regulatory approval and is expected to close around this time next year.
